sections.heading: KAUST Mathematics Competition (KMC): Regional Qualifier Practice Exercises

questions.q: [KAUST KMC — Regional Qualifier] By grouping consecutive perfect-square intervals along \( y = \sqrt{x} \) shown in the plot, compute the exact value of \[ \sum_{k=1}^{15} \lfloor \sqrt{k} \rfloor. \]
questions.answer: For each integer \( j \in \{1, 2, \dots, 3\} \), \( \lfloor \sqrt{k} \rfloor = j \) holds on \( j^2 \le k \le (j+1)^2 - 1 \), which contains \( 2j + 1 \) integers. Thus \[ \sum_{k=1}^{15} \lfloor \sqrt{k} \rfloor = \sum_{j=1}^{3} j(2j + 1) = \frac{(3)(4)(4\cdot 4 + 1)}{6} = 34. \]

questions.q: [KAUST KMC — Regional Qualifier] Let \( P(x) \) be a **monic** polynomial of degree \( 3 \) such that \( P(k) = 2k \) for every integer \( k \in \{1, 2, \dots, 3\} \). Find the exact value of \( P(4) \) (note the classic linear-extrapolation trap \( 8 \)!).
questions.answer: Define the auxiliary polynomial \( Q(x) = P(x) - 2x \). Since \( P \) is monic of degree \( 3 \ge 3 \), \( Q(x) \) is also monic of degree \( 3 \) and vanishes at \( 1, 2, \dots, 3 \). By the Factor Theorem, \[ P(x) - 2x = \prod_{k=1}^{3} (x - k). \] Substituting \( x = 4 \) yields \( P(4) = 6 + 2(4) = 14 \).

questions.q: [KAUST KMC — Regional Qualifier] Let \( P(x) \) be a polynomial of degree **at most** \( 2 \) satisfying \[ P(k) = \frac{24}{k} \quad \text{for } k = 1, 2, \dots, 3. \] Compute the exact value of \( P(4) \).
questions.answer: Clear denominators by setting \( Q(x) = x P(x) - 24 \), which has degree at most \( 3 \) and roots \( 1, 2, \dots, 3 \). Thus \( Q(x) = A \prod_{k=1}^{3} (x - k) \). Evaluating at the hidden anchor \( x = 0 \) gives \( -24 = A(-1)^{3} (3)! \implies A = 4 \). At \( x = 4 \), \( 4 P(4) - 24 = 24 \implies P(4) = 12 \).

questions.q: [KAUST KMC — Regional Qualifier] Let \( P(x) \) be a polynomial of degree **at most** \( 3 \) satisfying \[ P(k) = \frac{120}{k} \quad \text{for } k = 1, 2, \dots, 4. \] Compute the exact value of \( P(5) \).
questions.answer: Clear denominators by setting \( Q(x) = x P(x) - 120 \), which has degree at most \( 4 \) and roots \( 1, 2, \dots, 4 \). Thus \( Q(x) = A \prod_{k=1}^{4} (x - k) \).
